title: Pattern-Based Matrix Analysis Under Permutations
claim: A single framework covers many structural hypotheses, each expressible as a binary mask grouped into families of structure.
layout: 4 groups in 2x2 grid, 4 mask cells each, captions beneath
description: A 2x2 grid of labeled sections, each with a header rule and four square cells. Every cell is a binary mask drawn in dark blue on pale background, titled in bold above with an italic caption below naming the classical problem it models. Top-left, order and locality: banded, cyclic band, triangular, 2D grid stencil. Top-right, grouping and coupling: block-diagonal, block plus band, bordered block-diagonal, core-periphery. Bottom-left, hubs, nesting, intervals, localization: arrowhead, Ferrers, interval envelope, localized bicluster. Bottom-right, hierarchy, branching, self-similarity, bipartiteness: nested dissection, clique tree, Kronecker support, checkerboard. Daggers mark the families used in the experiments. The eye is drawn to the bold diagonal band and block shapes, and the repeating square layout gives a catalog look.
caption: Gallery of patterns, one representative per structural hypothesis (each cell is the binary mask $M$, blue $=1$), grouped by the kind of structure they encode: order, grouping, nesting, separability, branching, self-similarity. Daggers mark the families used in our experiments; Table [ref] gives the classical problem behind each pattern. Masks are shown up to the permutations the framework optimizes over (an anti-diagonal band equals a band under column reversal). Any binary mask is admissible: $M$ encodes the structure hypothesized for an application or is selected from a vocabulary.
abstract: Low-rank approximation captures one important notion of matrix simplicity: a matrix is simple if it is well described by a low-dimensional linear model. This paper studies a complementary notion. We consider matrices that become structurally simple only after permuting rows and columns, so that their mass concentrates in a prescribed geometric pattern such as a band, block-diagonal, arrowhead, or related form. We introduce a pattern distance that measures how close a matrix is to a given pattern after optimal reordering, giving a common framework for structural problems such as latent ordering, community detection, and bandwidth minimization. The problem is NP-hard in general; we derive an alternating algorithm based on Linear Assignment subproblems. We further introduce a pattern-plus-low-rank decomposition that combines permutation-structured fitting with a low-rank residual, whose permutation step is pattern fitting on the residual; its gains across pattern families persist at a matched parameter budget and are substantially reduced under a density-matched random-mask control. We evaluate the framework on synthetic recovery tasks, real correlation and graph adjacency matrices, and transformer attention heads, showing that a single universal algorithm recovers qualitatively different forms of matrix structure.
